newsitem.title: USA: U.S. declines to press for Ranariddh reinstatement.
newsitem.headline: U.S. declines to press for Ranariddh reinstatement.

text.p: The United States, citing Hun Sen's "military victory" in Cambodia, declined on Monday to insist that Prince Norodom Ranariddh, ousted by Hun Sen last week, be reinstated as first prime minister.

"There's no question that he (Hun Sen) has certainly achieved a major military victory, because he appears to have smashed the military forces of Prince Ranariddh," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
Senior U.S. officials met Ranariddh in Washington last Friday and still consider him first prime minister of Cambodia as a result of a U.N.-sponsored election in 1993, he said.
But "what we cannot do is get involved in party politics, in his own party's politics or in politics in Cambodia itself. I can't give you a prescription of what's going to happen," Burns said.
He said the United States "would like nothing better than the restoration of the status quo, meaning Prince Ranariddh could return and assume his place as first prime minister of Cambodia."

"But you have to separate the situation into what one hopes will happen -- which is restoration of the government -- vs. what one expects to happen now. Hun Sen ... I don't think has done much to indicate to Prince Ranariddh that it's safe to return," Burns added.

Hun Sen became second prime minister after losing the 1993 election and forcing himself into a coalition with Ranariddh. Hun Sen is now the sole power, but Washington is pressing at least for Ranariddh's royalist party to be brought back into the government.

The U.S. ambassador, Kenneth Quinn, after several days of trying, finally met with Hun Sen in Phnom Penh last weekend, and Burns said the envoy heard positive responses from Hun Sen on several issues of U.S. concern.

Hun Sen sought to legitimise his week-old government on Sunday by issuing a statement calling for the quick convening of parliament, the holding of "free and fair" elections, and the protection of human rights and a free press -- positions Washington had pressed him to embrace.

But Burns said, "... Frankly, when dealing with someone like that, in the wake of all these reports of the brutalities (political killings) of the last eight days, we're going to be much more impressed by his actions to put into place a liberal, democratic government than these nice words."
Burns declined to comment on reports from Beijing that Cambodian King Norodom Sihanouk had acquiesced in the coup by Hun Sen.
